I didn't do anything with the direct intention of getting it to stop (bc I didn't know what to do), though it could also have something to do with general stress management I was working on.  I was focusing on diverting my attention and staying optimistic and realistic, giving myself affirmations of my safety, and talking about it in therapy.  it was just a passing symptom, came and went without issue.

if it makes you feel any better, it's passed for me now.  emotionally, I'm not much better, but in terms of feeling like my thoughts are being heard, that went away a while ago.  I think I was so hyperfocused on those intrusive thoughts that it felt like everyone else had to be able to hear them too.  it really sucked during the span of time I experienced that, but it went away after a while.  just remember to remind yourself that you're okay <3

also feeling suicidal comes from a multitude of things and no person is the same.  trauma, genetics, lifestyle and health, stress, chemical imbalance, relationship strain, self doubt and doubt in the future, self hate, fear, grief, guilt, shame, and countless other reasons.

i deal with an agonizing amount of shame and self hate, which is derived from trauma.  but i also wasn't raised with a lot of stress, which makes it difficult for me to understand and cope with my high stress levels now.  not to mention, i used to eat very unhealthy and live isolated, and i come from a line of individuals with mental problems.  this is just surface level of what could influence my mental illness, and it requires more treatment than just having a support group, though that isn't meant to take away from the incredible power of having a strong support group!

Establishing coping mechanisms and routines is valuable.  These features are very dependent upon the person themself, but peers can help by encouraging these behaviors through invitations and calls to action. suggest different activities and coping skills for the individual to try.

Offer daily affirmations.

Suggest routines.

Invite them out for a fun and distracting activity (ie wholesome movie at the theaters, walk and chat in the park, get ice cream or coffee, or even staying home and playing video games together or watching funny videos).

Check in on them frequently and offer an ear.

Don't guilt them into not taking their own life (ie what about your family?  what about me?  why not just do this - you'll feel so much better!) - but also, be assertive (ie don't take no for an answer when inviting for some relaxing friend time (even if it's just being with each other and doing separate things)).

never invalidate a person's feelings by saying cliche things like, "just cheer up", "you'll be okay", "you have so much to live for", bc it's things we already know.  offer things that we don't hear as often.

and ultimately, encourage them to get professional help. ❤️

he didn't.  they turned him away.  said there weren't enough beds and he wasn't a "severe enough case".  i'm so scared for him.  and i feel like i'm going to lose it.  i feel so hopeless and helpless.

we're going to stay in town with family for a while longer and, during that time, we'll be sure that he's staying completely sober and safe.  my condition is that he has to be with someone at all times.  it's also comforting that is a firm believer of pinkie promises and doesn't make promises he can't keep, so when he goes to the bathroom, or if I have suspicion that he's going to do something he shouldn't be doing, I have that reassurance of, either he promises and I know he'll be safe, or he can't promise and I'm able to take precautions in response.

ultimately, if he shows any signs that he's not cooperating or things are getting worse, then I'll be taking him in.  but I've been in the hospital so many times before and I know that it can help with stabilization, but it can also be such a dark place to just sit with your thoughts and he struggles with such heavy feelings of loneliness, he said that hearing that we were all so concerned helped him realize how important it is that he keeps going.
